Arthurian Legend. A medieval cycle of stories centered on King Arthur, a quasi-historical British leader transformed into an iconic figure of chivalry, magic, and doomed nobility. Spanning centuries of literary retellings from Welsh folklore through French verse romance to modern fantasy, these tales explore themes of loyalty, ambition, betrayal, and the impossible quest for an ideal realm.

At the core of the tradition, Arthur appears as a once-and-future king, destined to return from death. Excalibur serves as his magical blade, and the Round Table as his symbol of unified, leaderless fellowship—a radical democratic ideal wrapped in courtly ritual. Merlin emerges as magician and counselor, the architect of Arthur's rise, though his own narrative grows increasingly tragic as the cycle progresses.

Lancelot stands as the greatest knight, yet also Arthur's greatest betrayer through his affair with Guinevere. He embodies the tragic tension between ideals and human weakness central to the legend. Morgan le Fay bridges the Christian and pagan worlds, sometimes Arthur's enemy sorcerer, sometimes his healer. She represents the magical forces that sustain and ultimately reclaim him.

The Holy Grail emerges as a central quest object in later versions, transforming the Arthurian cycle into a Christian allegory of spiritual seeking alongside martial heroism. Geoffrey of Monmouth's twelfth-century History of the Kings of Britain anchored the legend in a pseudo-historical framework that later authors expanded through French romance traditions. Avalon, the mythical island beyond reach, serves as both Arthur's birthplace and final resting place, making death itself ambiguous and Arthur's return eternally possible. The legend reflects and critiques medieval feudalism, kingship, and chivalric codes, making it as much a social commentary as a fantastical narrative.
